subsystems.name: Forward spectral models
subsystems.role: predict what an atmosphere would look like for a given mix of gases, clouds and temperature, so training data can be generated for worlds no telescope has yet measured.
parts: climate model for surface and vertical temperature structure

subsystems.name: Biosignature library
subsystems.role: a labelled catalogue of plausible spectra, split into biotic and abiotic classes, spanning wavelengths from the visible into the thermal infrared.
parts: abiotic control cases: CO2 worlds, steam atmospheres, hazy and cloudy planets
stellar and planetary parameter sampling grid

subsystems.name: Instrument simulator
subsystems.role: makes synthetic spectra look like real measurements, including their noise and artefacts.
parts: spectral resolution and wavelength coverage model (JWST covers roughly 0.6–28 µm across its instruments)
systematics: stellar contamination from spots and faculae, instrument drifts

subsystems.name: Classifier
subsystems.role: learns the boundary between biotic and abiotic spectra and outputs a probability rather than a yes/no verdict.
parts: feature attribution to show which gas bands drove the decision

subsystems.name: Calibration layer
subsystems.role: converts raw classifier output into honest probabilities, because a wrong 'yes' costs telescope time and credibility.
parts: Bayesian evidence comparison against retrieval fits

subsystems.name: Triage interface
subsystems.role: ranks candidate planets for scarce observing time and states the confidence behind each ranking.

buildSteps.title: Define the classes and the ground truth
buildSteps.detail: Decide which spectra count as biotic and which as abiotic. Only Earth provides a real biotic example, so the biotic class must be built from Earth's own spectrum and from models of early Earth, while the abiotic class spans CO2-dominated, steam, Titan-like and heavily hazed worlds.

buildSteps.title: Generate forward-model spectra
buildSteps.detail: Run radiative-transfer, chemistry and climate models across a wide grid of planet radius, surface pressure, stellar type, cloud coverage and haze. This yields tens of thousands to millions of synthetic spectra — the training set, because no labelled sample of inhabited exoplanets exists.

buildSteps.title: Inject instrument realism
buildSteps.detail: Convolve each spectrum to the resolution of a real spectrograph, add photon and detector noise at the expected signal-to-noise, and add stellar-contamination and systematic effects. Without this, a classifier learns clean model differences that never survive real data.

buildSteps.title: Train the classifier
buildSteps.detail: Split into training, validation and test sets, then train. Weight the sampling carefully: an unrepresentative prior will make the model report detections that reflect the training grid rather than the planet.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the output
buildSteps.detail: Test on held-out spectra, on planets outside the training distribution, and on known non-detections, then report performance as a false-positive rate at a fixed recall. Calibrated probabilities are the deliverable, not a verdict.

buildSteps.title: Validate against real measurements
buildSteps.detail: Apply the pipeline to actual spectra — Solar System planets, Earthshine, and exoplanets already observed — and confirm it flags known hazy, cloudy or spot-contaminated cases as abiotic rather than mislabelling them as life.

buildSteps.title: Embed in target triage
buildSteps.detail: Score candidate planets against the expected instrument, rank them for limited observing time, and publish the assumptions so a detection claim can be traced back to the models and priors that produced it.

prerequisites.why: transmission and emission spectra of rocky and sub-Neptune planets are now measured from space and from the ground; without spectra there is nothing to classify.

prerequisites.tech: Self-consistent forward models of planetary atmospheres
prerequisites.why: the models are good for known chemistry but must extrapolate to biospheres nobody has seen, and to unknown metabolisms that could produce gases Earth life does not.
oxygen with methane in disequilibrium is the best-studied signal, but abiotic routes to oxygen exist, so the labels themselves carry uncertainty.
exactly one inhabited planet is known, so every biotic label is either Earth's own spectrum or a model — the core limitation of the whole approach.

prerequisites.tech: Direct-imaging spectroscopy of temperate rocky planets
prerequisites.why: reflected-light spectra will test these classifiers on the planets they were designed for; a dedicated space telescope for that task is still a concept recommended by the 2020 astronomy decadal survey, not a built mission.
training and running the models is cheap; the harder need is shared, blinded benchmarks so different groups' classifiers can be compared fairly.

pathway.milestone: classifiers used in research to triage targets and speed up retrievals for JWST and ground-based observations
pathway.unlocks: a first practical filter for which planets are worth scarce observing hours.

pathway.milestone: community benchmark challenges and shared synthetic-plus-real test sets with published false-positive rates
pathway.unlocks: claims from different teams become comparable instead of incomparable.

pathway.milestone: pipelines coupled to direct-imaging instruments, so target lists and detection thresholds are set before observations begin
pathway.unlocks: observing time aimed at the worlds most likely to yield an interpretable answer.

pathway.milestone: a biosignature claim presented as a calibrated probability with a stated false-positive rate, backed by independent atmospheric lines
pathway.unlocks: the framework needed to argue credibly that a distant atmosphere contains life.
